Fossil fuel emitters and climate change: unpacking the governance activities of large oil and gas companies
Naghmeh Nasiritousi
Department of Political Science, University of Stockholm, Sweden

ABSTRACT Global climate change governance is under increasing pressure to deliver meaningful action. It is now widely agreed that a low-carbon growth path requires major transformations of energy systems. The ways in which the 10 largest oil and gas companies in the world present their rationales for addressing climate change and their activities related to climate action, including the oil and gas companies’ involvement in international climate diplomacy, are examined. How these major companies in diﬀerent world regions seek to inﬂuence states and other actors are illustrated through their actions on climate change. The analysis highlights the relations between state and non-state actors and our understanding of the allocation of responsibility in climate change politics. Novel empirical ﬁndings contribute to new insights into the climate change activities currently underway in the oil and gas sector, with implications for both the theory and practice of climate change governance.
KEYWORDS Oil and gas companies; climate change governance; private authority; non-state actors
Introduction

Private authority in environmental politics and governance has in recent years received growing interest, as states struggle to reach binding agreements on important environmental issues (Green 2013). In the realm of international climate change politics, there has been increasing attention on involving a range of non-state actors, including cities, businesses and NGOs, in eﬀorts to address climate change (Hoﬀmann 2011, Nasiritousi et al. 2016). However, the presence of large oil and gas companies at the international climate change conferences under the auspices of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has been the subject of increasing controversy.1 As one of the largest contributors of greenhouse gas emissions – from the production and consumption of the extracted oil and gas (Heede 2014) – they have been portrayed as lobbyists

Other studies point to diﬀerentiation between oil companies, with some employing more proactive strategies on climate change (van den Hove et al. 2002, Sæverud and Skjaerseth 2007). Most studies, however, examine oil companies based in Western countries, and there is limited knowledge about how these compare to the activities of oil and gas companies based in developing countries. With oil and gas companies having diﬀerent ownership structures and energy portfolios and facing diﬀerent regulatory and social pressures, it can be expected that their roles will vary in the area of climate change governance. On the other hand, the global political response to climate change increasingly places converging pressures across the sector (Levy and Kolk 2002). This means that there is a need to go beyond analyses that describe corporate political strategies as either proactive or reactive to instead examine the content of their strategies to better understand how these companies seek to inﬂuence instrument choice and policy design (Meckling 2015). With international eﬀorts to include new types of actors and partnerships in order to strengthen climate change governance,2 how might oil and gas companies address climate change issues, and can they contribute towards eﬀective global climate change governance?

Here, I examine how the 10 largest oil and gas companies in the world present their rationales for addressing climate change and their activities in this ﬁeld. I situate these activities in relation to UN climate multilateralism and transnational climate action. While a systematic comparison of these companies is beyond the scope of this discussion, I explore diﬀerences in their climate change activities depending on whether they are based in a developed or developing country, and whether the company is private or state-owned. I do so by studying their websites and conducting interviews with company representatives.

The next section establishes the importance of looking across a set of oil and gas companies on how they engage in climate change governance. Thereafter an analytical framework is presented to facilitate analysis of the governance activities of the companies in the area of climate change. After outlining the research design and methods used, the results are presented, before exploring the diﬀerences between companies based in developed vs. developing countries and those that are private vs. state-owned. The analysis of the major oil and gas companies’ self-reported climate change activities show that they are actively engaged in climate change governance at multiple levels, but to diﬀerent degrees and not always consistent with eﬀective climate change action. I conclude by discussing what the ﬁndings mean for how we understand the role of oil and gas companies in climate change governance.
Oil and gas companies and climate change governance

Global climate change governance has for more than 20 years centred around the intergovernmental negotiations under the auspices of the UNFCCC. These negotiations have focused on country-level eﬀorts to address climate change. With the top-down approach to international eﬀorts to address climate change being criticised for being ineﬀective (Victor 2011), there have been calls for non-state actors, such as cities, businesses and NGOs, to step in and take voluntary action. The mobilisation of a range of actors is considered necessary due to the gravity and complexity of the climate change challenge (Blok et al. 2012, Widerberg and Pattberg 2015).

Fossil fuel companies in particular have been singled out as needing to take responsibility for climate change (van den Hove et al. 2002). Heede (2014, p. 229) ﬁnds that ‘63% of cumulative worldwide emissions of industrial CO2 and methane between 1751 and 2010’ can be traced to 90 entities producing oil, natural gas, coal and cement. These entities are both investor-owned (private) and state-owned and are based in both developed and developing countries. All of the top 10 companies in terms of cumulative emissions are major oil and gas companies. These companies continue to hold fossil fuel reserves that, if burned, will contribute to intensifying climate change. According to McGlade and Ekins (2015), to limit global warming to 2°C, a third of oil reserves and half of current gas reserves should be kept in the ground.

Given their central position in the global carbon economy, what roles do major oil and gas companies play in global climate change governance? On the one hand, companies are not states and do not have a clear-cut place in governing climate change. On the other hand, non-state or private authority is important for understanding global governance outcomes (Falkner 2012, Green 2013). Non-state actors may aﬀect governance outcomes both indirectly by inﬂuencing states and other actors and directly through their own governance initiatives (Nasiritousi et al. 2016). This is particularly true for businesses that hold key positions in the global economy, as do major oil and gas companies. Moreover, some of the largest oil and gas companies are state-owned. While their non-state status can be questioned, state-owned companies do not have the status of a state under international law and are therefore by deﬁnition non-state entities. This highlights the need to see the non-state actor category as a spectrum, where some actors are clearly at the private end of the spectrum while others have diﬀerent degrees of attachment to public entities.

While the role of businesses in global climate change governance is well-researched (Levy and Newell 2005, Kolk and Pinkse 2007, Pinkse and Kolk 2012), there have been surprisingly few studies on the roles of major fossil fuel emitters. The notable exceptions focus on major oil and gas companies

based in developed countries (Levy and Kolk 2002, van den Hove et al. 2002, Sæverud and Skjærseth 2007). The omission of major oil and gas companies based in developing countries may be deliberate, since only developed countries took on emission reduction commitments under the Kyoto Protocol, meaning that companies headquartered in developed countries are likely to face greater pressures to address climate change. On the other hand, some of the largest oil and gas companies in terms of daily production are based in developing countries (Forbes 2012). Moreover, members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) are estimated to hold over 80% of the world’s reserves (OPEC 2015). An analysis that leaves out the activities of these large companies risks providing only a partial picture of the roles that major oil and gas companies play in climate change governance.

I therefore analyse the governance activities of the 10 largest (in terms of daily production) oil and gas companies in the world. According to Forbes (2012), these are (in descending order): Saudi Aramco, Gazprom, National Iranian Oil Co. (NIOC), ExxonMobil, PetroChina, BP, Royal Dutch Shell, Pemex, Chevron and Kuwait Petroleum Corp. (KPC) (see Table 1), all of which are among the world’s 15 largest contributors of greenhouse gas emissions cumulatively for years 1854–2010 (Heede 2014). Three (Shell, BP and Gazprom) are based in countries that took on emission commitments under the Kyoto Protocol, while two are American3 (ExxonMobil and Chevron). The remaining companies are based in countries that had no international legal obligations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions prior to the signing of the Paris Agreement in 2015. ExxonMobil, BP, Shell and Chevron are investor-owned companies, while the remainder are state-owned (fully or majority stake). These companies thus have in common their signiﬁcant contribution of greenhouse gases but diﬀer in terms of where they are based and operate as well as ownership structures. Rather than oﬀer a systematic comparison between these companies, my aim is to map their climate change activities and situate these in relation to UN climate multilateralism and transnational climate action. I do so by employing the governance proﬁle framework developed in Nasiritousi et al. (2016), as outlined in the next section.

One step in understanding how businesses aﬀect political outcomes is to examine corporate political strategies. Previous research has shown that the choice of corporate political strategy diﬀers depending on both interests and institutions, for example demonstrating that the strategic responses to climate change diverge between American and European oil and gas companies due to diﬀering institutional contexts and company histories, with the European companies being more proactive and the American companies more reactive (Levy and Kolk 2002, Meckling 2015). However, Meckling (2015) argues that there is a need to shift analytic focus to understand how corporate eﬀorts shape environmental policy rather than to simply determine whether corporations support or oppose environmental regulations.

One way to understand the diﬀerent roles that non-state actors play in climate change governance is through the concept of governance proﬁles. As developed in Nasiritousi et al. (2016), governance proﬁles map the level of recognition that diﬀerent types of non-state actors have gained in carrying out various governance activities. High recognition by a wider community is indicative of agency for that actor in that particular governance activity. The governance activities in focus for non-state actors are: inﬂuence the international climate change agenda; propose viable solutions to climate change; provide information and expertise; inﬂuence decisions and policymakers; raise awareness of climate change among the public; take actions on climate change mitigation; take action on climate change adaptation; evaluate consequences of policies and measures; represent public opinion on climate change issues; and represent marginalised voices.

Nasiritousi et al. (2016) found that businesses in general have gained recognition for their activities in inﬂuencing decisions and policymakers, inﬂuencing the international climate change agenda and taking mitigation action. Their weakest governance activities were perceived to be in raising awareness of climate change among the public and representing marginalised voices. The business representatives’ self-perceptions were high in proposing solutions and taking action on climate change mitigation and adaption.

I build on this work by unpacking the governance activities of the world’s 10 largest oil and gas companies to assess whether their activities follow the pattern identiﬁed in the governance proﬁle of businesses by Nasiritousi et al. (2016), and explore diﬀerences in how they work in the area of climate change governance. In contrast to Nasiritousi et al. (2016), this study does not focus on whether the companies have gained recognition for their actions from a wider community, but instead focuses on how the companies describe their own work.
This research design facilitates analysis of how these companies not only oppose or support environmental policies, but also how they undertake

hedging strategies, i.e. ‘corporate eﬀorts to shape environmental policy in favour of least-cost instruments and designs in the face of strong regulatory pressure’ (Meckling 2015, p. 20). By unpacking the governance activities of these companies, we can obtain a broader understanding of how they seek to participate in climate change politics and their roles in global climate change governance. While the roles of major Western oil and gas companies in opposing the Kyoto Protocol and spreading disinformation on climate change have been well-documented (Newell and Paterson 1998, Dunlap and McCright 2011, Falkner 2012, Downie 2014a), these roles, although signiﬁcant, are neither complete nor necessarily reﬂect how these companies act today. The governance activities framework allows for a wider mapping of their activities on climate change. The aim of the analysis is thus to illustrate what types of governance activities the companies are involved in and to tentatively map how these diﬀer between companies and regions.
Method

In order to explore the governance activities of the 10 major oil and gas companies, company websites were analysed and interviews were conducted with senior company representatives. The focus on the self-reported governance activities of the companies means that we gain an understanding of how the companies describe their own engagement with the climate change issue. While the information on the websites may be partial, and its content dependent on the companies’ transparency culture, websites generally oﬀer a rich source of information on a company’s activities as this is one of the key channels for communicating with policymakers, investors, other stakeholders and the general public. Thus, although the material on the websites is of varying quality, it generally provides an indication of the level of attention paid by the companies to climate change and provides examples of governance activities.

Company websites were searched during the ﬁrst half of 2015 for the terms ‘climate change’ and ‘global warming’ in English as well as in the original language where applicable.4 If these search terms did not return any results, the annual reports and the sustainability reports of the companies were read to ﬁnd the relevant information. Only one company website – NIOC – did not contain any information concerning climate change, and results for this company are thus entirely based on interview data.

The search results from the nine company websites were scanned for information relating to the diﬀerent governance activities outlined above. While most companies have a special webpage dedicated to climate change (or sustainability issues), the search went beyond these pages to also look at company speeches, reports, newsletters and other results. The search hits

numbered in the hundreds for each of the Western oil companies, around 50 for Gazprom and Pemex and 10 for Saudi Aramco. PetroChina and KPC’s website search functions did not return any hits and therefore their websites were searched manually. While some of the companies’ websites returned search results that stretched back more than a decade, the focus of this study is on the more recent governance activities, particularly post-COP15 (Copenhagen 2009).

In order to sort this information, a template was made where information relating to the companies’ general position on climate change, shareholder activism on climate change (where applicable) and their governance activities was collected and categorised under the diﬀerent governance activities. This required subjective interpretations of what the diﬀerent governance activities entail. For instance, attending and speaking at UNFCCC meetings has here been categorised as inﬂuencing the international climate change agenda, while it could alternatively be categorised as providing information and expertise, or inﬂuencing decisions and policymakers. Thus, the results presented below do not describe how the companies themselves would describe their governance activities; rather, they are an interpretation of the activities that they carry out as detailed on their websites. Nevertheless, these interpretations were made consistently across the diﬀerent companies, as seen in Table 2. The website search results thus provide an indication of the diﬀerent governance activities undertaken by the companies.

To gain deeper insights into the companies’ strategies and objectives, interview requests were sent to all 10 companies. One semi-structured interview was carried out in person with a company representative from Shell, one by phone with two representatives from Pemex and one by phone with a representative from an American company wishing to remain anonymous. All interviewees were senior company representatives working directly on climate change issues. Moreover, a telephone interview was conducted with a senior member of staﬀat the climate change division of the Ministry of Environment in Iran, who provided insights into the activities of the NIOC on issues of climate change. BP replied but declined to be interviewed, citing lack of resources to answer academic requests for interviews. Representatives from Gazprom and KPC ﬁrst agreed to participate but did not respond when sent written questions. The remaining companies did not respond to repeated interview requests.

The interview questions focus on how the companies engage on climate change, how their approach diﬀers from those of competitors, how they interact with domestic and international policymaking, whether the company has come under increasing pressure to take action on climate change in recent years and how it sees the company’s portfolio in terms of key energy sources in the future. The interviews thus provide additional details that contextualise the information found in the website search.

News articles and additional reports sometimes provide a diﬀerent picture than that presented by the companies themselves. While no systematic attempt has been made to validate the self-reported information from the oil and gas companies, these secondary sources are used to provide context to the presented information. Because these sources are predominantly from the Western world, however, less material is presented for non-Western companies.
Results: multiple roles, similar positions

On the whole, the results show that each of the oil and gas companies views climate change as a business risk and has therefore developed strategies to mitigate this risk. Table 2 presents the diﬀerent governance activities for the 10 oil and gas companies studied. Most companies appear to be active across the diﬀerent governance activities, with most activities centred around mitigation and inﬂuencing decisions and policymakers. The companies appear to be least active in representing marginalised voices, thus mirror the ﬁndings in Nasiritousi et al. (2016) on the governance proﬁle of businesses.

The question that follows from this is how do the companies carry out these governance activities, i.e. what is the content of their actions? In Table 2 examples of governance activities are presented, and companies associated with those examples are indicated. In other words, companies that highlight information related to each activity (either on their websites or through interviews) are shown in the table. This means that companies are mentioned for those examples that apply to that company, but the degree to which the companies are active within the governance activities will diﬀer. For instance, while both BP and KPC write that the companies take mitigation action through developing renewable energy sources, this activity is much more prominent, and discussed in greater detail, on the BP website than that of KPC. While some of the diﬀerence may be attributable to diﬀerent levels of detail in website content, much of it lies in a diﬀerence in substance as all companies have an incentive to present mitigation actions in their sustainability reports. Where a company has not been highlighted for a governance activity, this either indicates that the company does not engage in the activity or that it has not publicised that engagement. Shell’s website, for example, clearly states that they administer a political action committee in the USA, but since this information is not obviously visible on the other companies' web pages discussing climate change, Shell is the only company indicated in this category. Thus, as the analysis is based on self-reported information, the governance activities presented in Table 2 are not complete as some activities will be under-reported. Nevertheless, the results provide a ﬁrst mapping of governance activities of the 10 largest oil and gas companies through which we can gain new insights into how they engage on climate change.

In the following sections, these results will be elaborated using examples from company websites. First, the focus is on the governance activities, leaving analysis about how and why companies diﬀer to the next section. Below we start by examining the companies’ general positions on climate change and how this manifests itself in the activities that they are relatively active in, namely proposing solutions, inﬂuencing decisions and policymakers and the international agenda, taking mitigation action and providing information and expertise. Next we look at the governance activities that the companies appear to be less active in, namely raising awareness of climate change, taking adaptation action, evaluating consequences of policies and measures and representing public opinion and marginalised voices.
Climate change risk and its solutions according to the top 10 oil and gas companies

All investigated companies acknowledge that climate change poses a risk to society, but do so to diﬀerent degrees. European oil and gas companies were among the ﬁrst to acknowledge climate change, but American companies have followed suit, even though ExxonMobil still qualiﬁes its rationale by stressing that ‘there remains uncertainty in projecting future changes in climate and associated impacts’.5 Pemex and PetroChina acknowledge their responsibility to take action on climate change, while Saudi Aramco, Gazprom and KPC highlight climate change as an international problem that represents challenges and opportunities for their businesses. Gazprom considers that emission reductions are necessary for societies, but that targets toward decarbonising economies are political and based on ideological considerations.6

Almost all the companies thus emphasise that governments must strike a balance between reducing emissions and safeguarding economic growth and prosperity and present themselves as oﬀering solutions. The companies advocate cost-eﬀective solutions, with most agreeing that market mechanisms, greater reliance on natural gas as a lower-carbon fuel and carbon capture and storage (CCS) are viable solutions for climate change. ExxonMobil stands out for proposing a revenue-neutral carbon tax, arguing that cap-and-trade systems are ineﬃcient and therefore speak out against such regulation.7

The degree to which the companies advocate these solutions is however mixed. ExxonMobil has been criticised by its External Citizenship Advisory Panel for not making clear whether its proposal of a carbon tax is something that the company actively advocates.8 The European companies (BP and Shell) are the only companies actively and prominently lobbying in favour of carbon pricing; both have over the years signed several statements calling for a multilateral agreement on climate change that facilitates international carbon markets.9 Moreover, BP and Shell – along with four other major European oil and gas companies – in June 2015 sent letters to the

UNFCCC and the President of the COP21 Paris conference, as well as to the media, calling for the establishment of carbon pricing where it does not already exist and an international framework to link diﬀerent carbon markets.10 In the letter to the media they also highlight the role that natural gas can play in reducing emissions. Through these eﬀorts, the companies are calling on governments to adopt their preferred policy solutions, although their eﬀorts are weakened by the fact that only European companies subscribe to this call.11

Despite these advocacy eﬀorts in favour of climate action, oil and gas companies are involved in other advocacy eﬀorts that could be seen as undermining climate action. Chevron, for instance, has expressed unease with California’s climate policies, as these are viewed as too costly and threatening jobs.12 According to a speech by a company representative:

The potential impact of these regulations on our business is signiﬁcant. We’re working closely with the Governor and his administration to make sure this legislation is implemented in a rational, cost-eﬀective and equitable way. We’re also attempting to shape ongoing political discussions about climate change to ensure we take a rational path forward that balances economic and environmental needs.13

Similarly, a senior BP representative stated at the Brussels Forum in 2014 that: ‘Europe must rebalance its energy policy towards competitiveness and the provision of secure, aﬀordable energy, and not only lower carbon energy’.14
Examples of oil and gas companies working to weaken policies aimed at bringing down emissions have been highlighted elsewhere (Downie 2014b).15

This highlights the mixed advocacy strategies of these companies: the need for climate action is acknowledged, but implementation of speciﬁc measures is sometimes fought due to competitiveness concerns. These contradictions are also manifest in the trade associations that several of these companies are members of, some of which oppose most climate regulations.16

An initiative that has gained backing from companies based in diﬀerent regions (including BP, Pemex, Saudi Aramco and Shell) is the Oil and Gas Climate Initiative. Formally launched at the UN Secretary General’s Climate Summit in 2014, this initiative ‘aims to catalyse practical action on climate change in focus areas such as the role of natural gas, carbon reduction instruments and tools, and long-term energy solutions’.17

Through the sharing of best practices and industry collaboration, this initiative seeks to contribute to capacity building among its members to address climate change.18 Ahead of COP21 in Paris, the members presented a joint report highlighting their eﬀorts to address climate change (OGCI 2015) and issued a collaborative declaration calling for an eﬀective climate change agreement.19 Thereby, the companies seek to portray themselves as
constructively engaging with climate change, and voluntary, industry-driven initiatives as part of the solution.20

All companies have already introduced mitigation measures in their own operations. The most common measures are: investing in energy eﬃciency in own operations; gas gathering/reducing gas ﬂaring; establishing capabilities in CCS; research and development on technologies for more eﬃcient hydrocarbon production with reduced emissions; developing low carbon dioxide sources of energy, including natural gas; developing renewable energy; using an internal (proxy) carbon price to guide investments or screening projects for carbon risk; and helping customers use less energy and/or emit less carbon dioxide through products and services. However, as noted in stockholder proposals to the investor-owned companies, these measures have in many cases failed to bring down net emissions, and, in any case, the vast majority of the emissions stem from combustion of the fuels sold.21 Some companies acknowledge that even with these measures, net emissions are likely to rise as production moves to sources that are more energy-intensive.22

Most of the companies have registered commitments to take action on climate change on the UNFCCC’s NAZCA portal, with companies such as BP, Shell, Chevron, ExxonMobil, Gazprom and Pemex highlighting the use or intended use of an internal carbon price.23 However, shareholders of some of the investor-owned companies have criticised the unclear use of the carbon price in investment decisions, stating for example that they ‘are concerned that shareholder capital is at increasing risk from capital expenditures on high cost, high carbon projects that may become stranded’.24

The companies studied are all active through collaborations with others and some through initiatives such as the World Bank-led Global Gas Flaring Reduction Partnership or the Oil and Gas Methane Partnership of the Climate and Clean Air Coalition to take action on climate change mitigation. Several companies also address climate change through the International Petroleum Industry Environmental Conservation Association (IPIECA). These examples highlight the role of networks in forging common positions and approaches and the role of cooperation in spurring action.

By joining trade associations like IPIECA or the World Business Council on Sustainable Development, companies that are not part of a government delegation also gain the opportunity to be represented at UNFCCC negotiations.25

This illustrates a diﬀerence between investor-owned and state-owned companies, as representatives of the state-owned companies are part of the oﬃcial government delegations while those of investor-owned companies are there as observers. Most companies highlight their participation at UNFCCC meetings as a way to follow policy debates and to present information at side-events or exhibits. They are thus all active at the international policy level, although their

level of involvement diﬀers. Shell attends on a regular basis and sends several representatives, while Gazprom is less consistently active. Shell representatives participate actively in exchanges and dialogues; for instance a Shell representative addressed a Technical Expert Meeting on Carbon Capture Use and Storage at the Bonn conference in October 2014, presenting their current work using this technology and stressing that CCS is needed to achieve zero net emissions.26 Both Chevron and Saudi Aramco have, like Shell, actively promoted CCS at these meetings. Saudi Aramco’s environment newsletter points out how they have worked ‘through the proper channels to include CCS in project activities of the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) of the Kyoto Protocol’.27 The UNFCCC is thus viewed as an important venue for the exchange of views with international policymakers and other stakeholders.

The CCS example highlights how these companies’ expertise is sought by policymakers to make informed choices. Similarly, a Chevron representative has been involved as a review editor in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Special Report on Carbon Dioxide Capture and Storage and has contributed to other IPCC reports (Chevron 2006). The provision of information and expertise is thus one way in which these companies can aﬀect how problems and solutions are perceived.

The centrality of oil and gas in the energy mix and the need for cost-eﬀective solutions are the key messages that unite all the companies in their governance activities on climate change. The unpacking of governance activities shows that the companies employ a mix of opposition, hedging and support strategies as they engage in environmental politics (cf. Meckling 2015).
Additional engagement by some oil and gas companies

While the diﬀerent companies address climate change to diﬀerent degrees, they are unanimous that oil and gas represent vital resources and that they will remain so in the foreseeable future. Many companies highlight that due to demand growth for energy as developing countries grow richer, all energy sources must be developed. The ﬁrst paragraph of Shell’s website designated to climate change states: ‘Population growth and economic development are driving up energy demand. All energy sources will be needed, with fossil fuels meeting the bulk of demand’.28 Most companies stress the beneﬁts of energy production to societies in terms of economic growth and well-being and argue that climate change policies should be designed so as not to hurt citizens.29 Thus, they appear to be taking on the role of representing the voice of the average consumer. Moreover, some companies present long-term energy scenarios in major reports, evaluating policies and measures. All these reports – ExxonMobil’s Outlook for Energy,31 BP’s Energy Outlook32 and Shell’s Scenarios33 – anticipate demand for energy to grow in the future and highlight the continuing important role of oil and gas in meeting demand growth. A few companies have also launched initiatives on climate education or use their websites or other social media to inform customers about energy issues, typically by highlighting the company’s position. Pemex writes that it has over several years participated in the World Wildlife Fund’s Earth Hour Initiative by switching oﬀlights at its Executive Tower and other corporate oﬃces at the main oil centres in Mexico (Pemex 2011). Similarly, Saudi Aramco highlights that they engage in public education: ‘Millions of Saudis received energy-eﬃciency tips through our public awareness programs’.34

A majority of the companies have also begun to develop adaptation plans for key production assets to remain resilient. Gazprom highlights ‘thermal eﬀects on the permafrost’ as a potential risk to its pipelines and states that the company is likely to face higher costs for repair and recovery as well as construction of infrastructure as a result of climate change impacts (Gazprom 2008/2009, 2010). Similarly, Pemex highlights that, due to sealevel rises and an increased number of extreme weather events, it is implementing actions to reduce vulnerability (Pemex 2013). Thus, these companies recognise the risks of climate change to their businesses.

In sum, the analysis of the governance activities of the major oil and gas companies shows that they appear to be involved in climate change governance at multiple levels, albeit to diﬀerent degrees, with several being both active in deﬁning the problem and oﬀering solutions.
Discussion: how and why companies diﬀer on climate change activities

As is evident from Table 2, there are clear diﬀerences between how the major oil and gas companies engage with climate change. Generally, the investor-owned companies, particularly in Europe, appear to be active across a greater number of governance activities than national oil companies in developing countries. Particularly companies such as KPC and NIOC appear to be engaged mostly on aspects of climate change work that are cost-eﬀective, such as energy eﬃciency programmes and other technical solutions that can oﬀer savings. Given that developing countries

have historically not had binding reduction targets, this is not surprising, as these companies have lacked a legal incentive to get involved in climate change work. The table nevertheless shows that some companies in developing countries are relatively active in positioning themselves as taking action, despite their countries not having had legal obligations to reduce emissions.

Interviewees were asked why there are diﬀerences in the climate change activities of oil and gas companies depending on whether they are based in a developed or developing country, and whether the company is private or state-owned. All pointed to three overarching factors explaining these diﬀerences: national policies; resources and capacity; and company-level factors, such as the management level. The investor-owned companies also highlighted additional pressures from NGOs and shareholders. The American company representative said that national oil companies ‘don’t have to respond to shareholders, they don’t have to respond to college and university students on divestment’. Similarly, the Shell representative said that many national oil companies have ‘little capacity or interest in the subject [of climate change]’, one reason for this being that national oil companies are not ‘subject to nearly as much NGO scrutiny and criticism as IOCs [international oil companies]’. He described Greenpeace as well as the Carbon Tracker Initiative, which popularised the term ‘carbon bubble’,35 as prominent in putting pressure on international oil companies.

That national oil companies come under less pressure on climate change from NGOs is conﬁrmed by a Pemex representative, who described diﬀerent sorts of pressure to take action on climate change, mentioning foremost internal pressures in the organisation ‘to be more eﬃcient and to try to reduce emissions’, but also social and international pressure, including from being members of partnerships that require the company to demonstrate results. A Pemex representative also said that, on a general level, the diﬀerence between national and private oil and gas companies stems from diﬀerences in resources and capacities related to technology and knowledge.

The American company representative also stressed that many national oil companies have very little capacity, they even want to learn from us on how to do certain things like internal carbon pricing, adaptation, […] so they are like a decade behind. […] I can tell that they don’t have much infrastructure inside the company to deal with climate change.
However, he qualiﬁed this by saying:

The only exception […] could be, Saudi Aramco. Aramco is very rich and they are a sovereign government that can throw billions of dollars to projects as they wish. So they’ve built up teams over the years, so I think Aramco is the one that’s most ready to do things and they are doing things.

The Saudi case, he said, is interesting because the company is actually more progressive than its government has been at international negotiations.36 On the whole, however, national-level policies, resources and capacity, as well as company-level factors, such as how the management of the company assesses opportunities and strategic interests, appear to play a role in explaining the diﬀerent levels of engagement with climate change among major oil and gas companies. Although based on only four interviews, it conﬁrms ﬁndings from previous studies (e.g. Levy and Kolk 2002, Sæverud and Skjærseth 2007).
Additional diﬀerences between the major oil and gas companies

While national oil companies appear mostly focused on implementing policies, investor-owned companies also emphasise the importance of shaping the discussion on climate change. This is because national oil companies have an intricate relationship with the state and do not have the same need to legitimise their positions in the eyes of the public. The interviewees with insights into Pemex and NIOC (both national oil companies) stressed that the companies work according to plans decided by government, although a Pemex representative stressed that they also seek to get involved in additional initiatives and partnerships to attract resources for projects to reduce emissions. Thus, national oil companies get their mandates from government, but can inﬂuence this mandate in both its formulation and its implementation. A key part of their work, according to the interviewees, is to implement low-carbon solutions and become more eﬃcient in the use of energy, as this will also lead to savings that will beneﬁt the company. While supporting government policies, which also include providing technical support to government negotiators at UNFCCC conferences, a Pemex representative mentioned that they have continuing conversations with the government on energy policies and have had success in arguing for the inclusion of carbon credits in national legislation on climate change. So the focus in these companies is more on implementation and policy development rather than engaging a wider audience to discuss energy issues.
This can be contrasted with the Shell representative, who described how the company works both on the policy arena and what he calls the discussion arena:

we engage in the development of policy at a national level in particular, we like to see things like the EU ETS appear and develop and work. Just as an example over the last two years we have been very active supporting what […] is called the market stability reserve to get the ETS back to a viable and meaningful carbon price. So we’re active in the policy arena, but we’re also active in the sort of discussion arena – the arena where people try to understand this issue. And we do that through instruments such as our scenario planning. What does it mean, what does 2 degrees C mean, how does the

energy system respond, what happens over time? All of these things, I think many people don’t really have a grip on. I think the energy companies need to play a role in helping people understand where we are and where potentially we could go.

The American company representative, while highlighting that the company is ‘low-key’ on these issues, also discussed the importance of educating policymakers and other stakeholders. Describing the company’s role at UNFCCC meetings, he said that holding side-events is a way to educate negotiators, stressing that educating should not be confused with lobbying:
We’re not telling negotiators what to do, we’re just telling them the options, what the options look like and what pros and cons, costs beneﬁts all that.

The shaping of information and ideas through the employment of discursive power (Falkner 2012) is thus much more prominent for investor-owned companies as the relationship with states and society is diﬀerent compared to national oil companies. Western oil companies’ important role in shaping information and ideas on climate change has been highlighted in previous literature focusing on ExxonMobil’s spreading of disinformation (e.g. van den Hove et al. 2002). In their 2011 Corporate Citizenship Report, ExxonMobil highlighted that: ‘We have ceased funding groups we believe were addressing the public policy discussion by questioning the science of climate change as opposed to exploring solutions to this complicated challenge’ (ExxonMobil 2011, p. 25).37 More recently, Ben van Beurden, Chief Executive Oﬃcer of Shell, emphasised that an important role for the industry is to ‘oﬀer some realism and practicality to the debate about climate change’.38 Calling on the industry to be more assertive, he said: ‘Fossil fuels out, renewables in – too often, that’s what it boils down to. Yet in my view, that’s simply naïve’.39 Through speeches by company leaders, brieﬁngs and reports, many major oil and gas companies seek to inﬂuence how climate change and possible solutions are perceived. The shaping of information can also take place through the sponsorship of think tanks, NGOs or other institutions, and major oil and gas companies can thus play a role in setting the tone of the debate surrounding climate change, demonstrating their discursive power.

Taken together, major oil and gas companies have important roles to play in climate change governance, but whether they will play a constructive role is yet to be determined. Asked about the anticipated key energy sources in their company’s portfolio in the next 20 years, all the interviewees answered oil and gas, as this is where they have their core business and capabilities. Much emphasis appears to be placed on CCS as a solution to lower emissions from fossil fuel production, although some companies acknowledge that carbon dioxide injection can be used to enhance oil recovery.40 Others highlight uncertainties regarding its technical and

commercial feasibility (BP 2013), with ExxonMobil stating that ‘CCS is not the perfect answer’ to reducing global CO2 emissions.41 It is also telling that all the investor-owned companies have stated on their websites that they do not view as realistic that policymakers introduce measures that will set the world on a path to reach the 2°C goal.42 On the other hand, oil and gas companies are aware of the risks associated with climate change and have introduced various measures to deal with this risk.
Conclusion

Oil and gas companies are key actors on climate change as they are among the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions as controllers of large fossil fuel outputs (Heede 2014). The 10 largest oil and gas companies in the world in terms of daily production have to diﬀerent degrees acknowledged their responsibility to take action on climate change and are involved in a range of governance activities in multiple arenas. They appear to be most active in inﬂuencing policymakers and decisions, as well as taking mitigation action, which mirrors ﬁndings about the role of the business sector in climate change governance (Nasiritousi et al. 2016). The analysis of governance activities thus indicates that by working with governments, but also beyond governments, these companies are involved in supporting, undermining, changing and/or reducing the pressure for new government policies. This illustrates a need to more closely analyse how companies engage on climate change beyond the traditional support or reject dichotomy. Moreover, the rosy picture of non-state actors often depicted in the literature either as defenders of the public good or as actors that can spur more eﬀective actions, for example in terms of bridging the emissions gap (Biermann and Gupta 2011, Hoﬀmann 2011, Blok et al. 2012), is thus only part of the story. The study also showed interesting diﬀerences in governance activities on climate change across the companies. The investor-owned companies based in developed countries face additional pressures to take action from NGOs and shareholders, and engage across more governance activities. They are also more likely to employ discursive power to seek to frame the debate (Falkner 2012). Despite not having had any legal obligations to reduce emissions, several companies based in developing countries are actively engaged with climate change. Similarities within the sector illustrate the converging pressures that the global political response to climate change has generated (Levy and Kolk 2002). Some of the converging and diverging pressures for taking action on climate change faced by diﬀerent types of oil and gas companies are thus exempliﬁed.

I have oﬀered a novel approach to analysing the business–global governance nexus. Analysis of governance activities illustrates that business engagement in global climate governance amounts to more than self-

regulation and traditional lobbying to include multiple interactions at diﬀerent governance levels. UNFCCC conferences are described as an important convening forum by most companies, with interviewees appreciating opportunities to share perspectives with policymakers and other stakeholders. Moreover, private sector partnerships, such as the Oil and Gas Climate Initiative, illustrate how transnational initiatives spread best practices and provide a platform for action. These ﬁndings are in line with literature that describes how multiple spheres of authority have emerged in climate change governance, highlighting the complex links between actors and levels of governance (Pattberg and Stripple 2008).

While I have focused on the governance activities as reported by the companies themselves and do not seek to verify the information, I have broadened the picture of oil and gas companies beyond that of lobbyists against climate change legislation and funders of organisations that discredit climate science. The unpacking of their governance activities has focused attention on the contents of their strategies on climate change, showing a relatively concerted eﬀort to promote natural gas but more disagreement about the feasibility of CCS. This type of analysis thus brings new insights into the hedging strategies of these companies. As a next step, the agency of these actors should be studied to see where their actions have important eﬀects on the ground. Moreover, if global climate change governance is moving toward the direction of greater involvement of non-state actors, this raises questions about the implications of their involvement on the legitimacy of evolving governance arrangements, the answer to which remains inconclusive in the literature and requires further empirical work (Widerberg and Pattberg 2015).

With global climate change governance becoming decentralised and the focus shifting to nationally determined contributions, and as the pressure for stronger climate change action continues to grow, the evolving engagement of major oil and gas companies in climate change governance will be increasingly important.
